blocks.text: The transport of sugars in plants takes place through phloem tissue. Passive theories of phloem transport include:
Diffusion is far too slow, to account for the velocities of sugar movement in phloem, which on the average is 1 meter per hour, while the rate of diffusion is 1 meter per eight years.

Pressure flow theory: The pressure-flow theory, also known as the mass-flow hypothesis, is the most widely accepted explanation for the transport of sugars in plants through the phloem. This process of translocation moves sugar from the source (where they are synthesized) to the sink (where they are consumed or stored). This theory was proposed by Ernst Munch in 1930. This theory relies on the principle of osmotic pressure differences between source and sink regions. Following steps explain the pressure-flow theory.

items: The glucose formed during photosynthesis in mesophyll cells, is used in respiration. The excess of glucose is converted into non-reducing sugar i.e., sucrose.

Sucrose is actively transported from mesophyll cells to the companion cells of phloem. From here, sucrose diffuses to sieve tubes, through plasmodesmata. So, the concentration of sucrose in sieve tubes increases.

Due to higher sucrose (solute) concentration in sieve tubes, water moves into them by osmosis from the nearby xylem of leaf. It results in an increase in the water potential at the source end of sieve tubes.

At the sink end, sugar is actively unloaded from sieve tubes and water also follows by osmosis. The exit of water lowers the water potential at the sink end. So, there is a higher water potential at the source end while a lower water potential at the sink end.
The difference in water potential causes water to flow from source to sink. Since sucrose is dissolved in water, it is carried along from source to sink along with water.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: These steps confuse water potential with pressure. Loading sucrose lowers the water potential in the sieve tube at the source, which is why water enters from the xylem; the water that enters raises the hydrostatic (turgor) pressure there. At the sink, water leaves with the sugar and the pressure falls. This pressure difference, not a water-potential difference, pushes the sap from source to sink, as Figure 8.11 shows.

blocks.alt: A xylem column on the left and a phloem sieve tube in the middle, with a leaf (source of sucrose) and its companion cell at the top right and a fruit (sink for sucrose) with its companion cell at the bottom right; plasmodesmata join the companion cells to the sieve tube.

Numbered steps: 1 sugar made in the leaf; 2 sucrose actively loaded into the companion cell and sieve tube; 3 water enters the sieve tube from the xylem by osmosis (higher hydrostatic pressure); 4 sucrose actively unloaded into the fruit and water follows (lower hydrostatic pressure); 5 bulk flow of solution down the sieve tube. Legend: water, sucrose, osmosis, active transport of sucrose.
